lesson.title: mir / dir / ihm Pronoun Gym
lesson.subtitle: Twenty give/tell/thank drills with the receiver pronouns

hook.title: The Receiver Circuit
hook.content: Three pronouns, four verbs, real sentences. Gib mir das Buch. Ich danke dir. Ich helfe ihm. Es gefällt mir. That is the entire gym — and every rep is a sentence Germans say daily. The skill is reflex-speed: receiver in the sentence? → mir/dir/ihm, not mich/dich/ihn. The trap is that English uses the SAME pronoun forms for both jobs (I thank you / you thank me), so your instinct reaches for the accusative. The circuit retrains it.

footnotes.title: The One-Syllable Rule of Thumb
footnotes.content: After geben, danken, helfen, gefallen, sagen (to!), and the prepositions mit, bei, zu, von, aus, nach, seit — the receiver answers in dative: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen. Notice mir/dir both end in -r: the dative's signature, the r of 'for'.

pattern.title: The Circuit
pattern.content: Round one — giving: Gib mir das Salz. Er gibt ihr das Buch (ihr — to her, the feminine dative). Round two — thanking: Ich danke dir und du dankst mir. Round three — helping: Wir helfen ihm. Round four — pleasing: Das gefällt mir (that falls well to me — 'I like that'). Round five — commanding: Sag mir! — tell me! Five rounds, three pronouns, permanent reflex.
pattern.linguist_note: The full dative pronoun set: mir, dir, ihm, ihr (to her), uns, euch, ihnen. English mirrors it scattered: me, thee, him, her, us, you, 'em — the same case, half-buried.

exercises.prompt: Circuit round one — match the receiver sentences:
exercises.target_answer: Gib mir das Buch, Ich danke dir, Wir helfen ihm, Das gefällt mir
exercises.meaning: give me the book, I thank you, we help him, I like that
exercises.explanation: Every receiver takes the dative: mir, dir, ihm — the giving case in action.

exercises.prompt: Trap check: 'Ich sehe ___.' (I see HIM — direct object!):
exercises.explanation: sehen acts directly on its object — accusative ihn. helpen-style receiver verbs take ihm; seeing takes ihn.

exercises.meaning: Ich helfe ihr = I help her (to-her)
exercises.explanation: ihr is the feminine dative — 'to her'. helfen demands it; sie would be the accusative.

exercises.prompt: Select EVERY honest English rendering of this Dative sentence:
exercises.german: Ich gebe dem Bruder das Buch
renderings: I give the brother the book
I give the book to the brother
I am giving the brother the book
traps: The brother gives me the book
I gave the brother the book
exercises.target_answer: I give the brother the book
exercises.meaning: I give the brother the book
exercises.explanation: 'dem Bruder' carries the 'to the brother' role inside the article 'dem' itself — English can express it either by word order or with 'to'. [Ref: Sie hilft ihm heute]

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "Give me the salt please"

vocab_hints.note: geben → gib! — the command chops the -en; with e-_added: Gib mir!

exercises.explanation: Command + dative receiver + accusative thing + bitte — the four-part table sentence of every German kitchen.
cues: Start with "Gib" and anchor "mir" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Use mir/dir/ihm/ihr/Ihnen at reflex speed with geben, danken, helfen, gefallen.
summary.takeaway: Receiver in the sentence → dative pronoun. Sehen takes ihn; helfen takes ihm — the verb decides, the case obeys.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Dative Verbs — helfen, danken, gefallen — the club that refuses the accusative.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from mir / dir / ihm Pronoun Gym (Give me the salt please):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Gib mir das Salz bitte" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of mir / dir / ihm Pronoun Gym without relying on short-term echo.

mir.context_translation: Can you please help me? (literally: help to me)
mir.etymology_derivation: Dative of ich — the same ancient pronoun as English me, keeping the 'to me' meaning (mir ist kalt = it is cold to me). [wiktionary]

dir.etymology_derivation: Dative of du — the exact twin of archaic English 'I give it thee'; the dative is the giving case. [wiktionary]

ihm.etymology_derivation: Dative of er — the exact twin of English him; the h dropped from speech and stayed in spelling. [wiktionary]

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

danken.etymology_derivation: Danke is an ellipsis of "[Ich] danke [dir/Ihnen]".

helfen.etymology_derivation: p → f. Governs the dative case (mir).

gefallen.context_translation: I like it (it falls well to me).
gefallen.etymology_derivation: ge- + fallen — 'to fall to someone' (by lot or liking), like English 'as it falls out'. Strong verb: gefiel, gefallen. [wiktionary]

grad.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French grade, Latin gradus 'a step' — the same Latin source as English grade/degree. [wiktionary]

kasse.context_phrase: Bitte zahlen Sie an der Kasse.
kasse.etymology_derivation: From Italian cassa, Latin capsa — the same Latin root behind English case and cash. [wiktionary]

bohne.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic bauno; English bean is a direct cognate with the same meaning. [wiktionary]

klug.context_phrase: Das Mädchen ist klug und freundlich.
klug.context_translation: The girl is clever and friendly.
klug.etymology_derivation: From Middle Low German klok via the Lower Rhineland, Proto-Germanic *klokaz; cognates include Old Norse klokr and dialectal Dutch kloek. Standard English has no cousin of this word. [wiktionary]

gummi.context_translation: The ball is made of rubber.
gummi.etymology_derivation: Borrowed in the 13th century from Medieval Latin gummi, from Greek kommi, ultimately Egyptian - the same chain that gave English gum. [wiktionary][etymonline]

apotheke.context_phrase: Ich hole das Rezept in der Apotheke.
apotheke.context_translation: I get the prescription at the pharmacy.
apotheke.etymology_derivation: Ultimately from Ancient Greek apothēkē (storehouse) — the same Greek word that gave English apothecary, twin borrowings; German doublets are Boutique and Bodega. [wiktionary]

postkarte.context_phrase: Wir schreiben eine Postkarte von Rom.
postkarte.context_translation: We are writing a postcard from Rome.
postkarte.etymology_derivation: Post + Karte, both documented twins (post, and Karte the twin of card) — a post-card, word for word. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
